title: Palms (Matthew 21:1–11)
hookLine: he rides in on a donkey and the crowd throws coats on the road

lines: COATS AND BRANCHES ON THE ROAD.
cards: Picture a parade. Presidents arrive in armored cars. Conquering generals in Rome rode in chariots, and kings entered cities on war horses.

Everybody could see the power. Now it's springtime, just before Passover, and Jerusalem is packed with pilgrims. Jesus sends two disciples to a village on the Mount of Olives to fetch something for his entrance.
Not a horse. A donkey, and her colt. They throw their cloaks over them, and he sits on them.
The crowd goes wild. They spread their coats on the road and lay down branches cut from the trees. And they shout one word, over and over.

teach.b: The crowds cry out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest."
Hosanna comes from Hebrew, from a line in Psalm one hundred eighteen: hoshia na: save us, please.

teach.h: A CRY FOR HELP BECOMES A CHEER.
teach.b: It began as a cry for help and became a shout of praise, like a cheer. Both meanings are in the air that day: help us, and hooray. The donkey is no accident.

teach.h: A KING, MEEK, ON A DONKEY.
teach.b: Matthew says it fulfills the prophet Zechariah: "Behold thy king cometh to thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass." A king, but a meek one, who comes in peace, not on a war horse.

The whole city is stirred up, asking: who is this? And the crowds answer: this is Jesus the prophet, from Nazareth of Galilee. The Church relives this day every year on Palm Sunday, the start of Holy Week.

Palms are blessed, and people carry them in procession into the church. Then, in the same Mass, the whole Passion is read, and the mood turns: the crowd's hosanna and the cross, held together on one day.

teach.h: PALMS BLESSED, THEN BURNED FOR ASHES.
teach.b: Many Catholics take their blessed palms home, tuck them behind a crucifix, and bring them back the next year, when old palms are burned to make the ashes for Ash Wednesday.

teach.h: BLESSED IS HE THAT COMETH IN THE NAME OF THE LORD.
teach.b: And at every Mass, all year, Catholics sing this crowd's words in the Holy, Holy, Holy: hosanna in the highest.

how: On Palm Sunday Catholics receive blessed palms, walk in procession, and hear the Passion read; many keep the palms at home until they are burned for the next Ash Wednesday, and every Mass sings hosanna in the Sanctus.

o: Hebrew for save us, please: a plea that became praise
Hebrew for peace, an everyday greeting and blessing
Hebrew for king, a title for David's royal heirs

games.q: you're about to enter the capital city at the height of the festival, and everyone expects a king. what do you ride?
o: a war horse, so the city sees your power.
nothing. you slip in quietly on foot.
games.why: a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah: “Behold thy king cometh to thee, meek, and sitting upon an ass.”

practice: Think about who arrives in your day: a child home from school, a coworker walking in late, a neighbor, a stranger at the door; most arrivals get a glance, or nothing.

Choose one person and picture giving them a real welcome, eyes up, a smile, their name: not a parade, just a coat on the road. If you pray, you can say the crowd's word, hosanna, as praise or as a cry for help.

wordCard.voice: Hosanna. From Hebrew: save us, please. A cry for help that became a shout of praise, sung at every Mass. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: save, please. From Psalm 118:25; in Greek it became hōsanna.

carryVoice: Your line: a king on a donkey. Power that comes in peace. Day fifty-seven, and Holy Week begins.
